stated: Reform UK will abolish IR35 rules to support sole traders, acknowledging that self-employed individuals often work longer hours and take more risks without pension or sick pay benefits.

source.quote: Abolish IR35 Rules to Support Sole Traders Britain’s self-employed often work longer hours and take more risks. Many have no pension and receive no sick pay.

bearing_set.reason: IR35 abolition directly affects the earning arrangements, take-home income, and working conditions of contractors and sole traders — squarely a good-work-and-fair-pay question about whether self-employed people can earn a decent, secure living through their chosen working structure.

Contractors and freelancers currently caught by IR35 pay employer-equivalent NICs and are taxed as employees; abolition would materially raise their real disposable income via a lower effective tax/NICs burden — a direct movement in the O2 disposable-income indicator for a large, identifiable group.
Abolishing IR35 directly reduces the tax and NI burden for contractors operating through personal service companies, materially raising their take-home pay — the core O11 indicator.

IR35 generates significant HMRC revenue by aligning tax treatment of disguised employees with employees; abolition removes that revenue stream, widening the fiscal gap with no stated offset — a concrete worsening of the funded/borrowed balance.
The beneficiaries of IR35 abolition are disproportionately higher-earning professional contractors; the distributional incidence is regressive, plausibly widening the income/wealth gap.

membership_note: IR35 is fundamentally a tax-treatment rule; abolition primarily bears on take-home pay (O11), public revenue sustainability (O12), and distributional fairness (O14), with a real but secondary labour-market quality spillover (O4) via the bogus-self-employment incentive mechanism.
